conflicts/camisard-war/name: The Camisard War of the Cévennes Huguenots
conflicts/camisard-war/religionRoleNote: The Camisards rose to restore the Reformed worship outlawed by the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), were led and directed by 'inspired' prophets, and targeted priests, churches and Catholic symbols; religion was both the stated and the real cause. Historians such as Philippe Joutard and W. Gregory Monahan have also shown the role of rural poverty, war taxation (the capitation of 1695) and regional resentment of royal intendants, and Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie placed the revolt within the long history of Languedoc peasant unrest. These factors shaped who joined and when, but the movement's identity, aims and language were overwhelmingly religious.
conflicts/camisard-war/sides/0/faith: Reformed Protestant (Huguenot), with a strong prophetic movement
conflicts/camisard-war/sides/1/name: Royal government of Louis XIV and Catholic militias
conflicts/camisard-war/sides/1/leaders/1: Nicolas de Lamoignon de Basville, intendant of Languedoc
conflicts/camisard-war/summary: A guerrilla rising of Protestant peasants and artisans in the mountains of the Cévennes against Louis XIV's suppression of Protestantism. Led by young lay preachers and prophets who spoke in states of ecstatic inspiration, the Camisards fought royal armies to a standstill in 1702–04, burning churches and killing priests, while the crown responded with executions, massacres and the systematic burning of upland villages. The main revolt ended in 1704–05, with sporadic resistance until 1710.
conflicts/camisard-war/story:
The Edict of Nantes (1598) had granted French Protestants limited toleration, but Louis XIV progressively restricted it, sent dragoons to be billeted on Protestant households (the dragonnades of 1681–85) and finally revoked it by the Edict of Fontainebleau in October 1685. Protestant worship was forbidden, pastors were expelled on pain of death, while lay people were forbidden to emigrate and declared 'new converts' to Catholicism. Perhaps 150,000–200,000 Huguenots fled abroad nonetheless. In the Cévennes and Bas-Languedoc, where Protestants formed the majority in many communities, people continued to meet in secret assemblies in the 'Desert'. Lay preachers such as Claude Brousson, executed at Montpellier in 1698, kept the faith alive, and troops broke up assemblies, killing or sending participants to the galleys.

From the late 1680s a prophetic movement spread from the Dauphiné and the Vivarais into the Cévennes. Young men, women and even children fell into trances, trembled, and spoke in the language of Scripture, calling for repentance and announcing the fall of 'Babylon', meaning the Catholic Church. Pierre Jurieu, the exiled pastor in Rotterdam, had predicted from the book of Revelation that the restoration of French Protestantism would come in 1689. The authorities treated the prophets as dangerous fanatics, imprisoning and executing many of them.

On the night of 24 July 1702 a band of about fifty Protestants led by the prophet Esprit Séguier attacked the house of the abbé François de Langlade du Chaila, archpriest of the Cévennes and inspector of missions, at Le Pont-de-Montvert, where he held prisoners captured on their way to emigrate. They freed the prisoners and killed du Chaila, then killed several other priests and Catholic notables. Séguier was captured and burned alive at Le Pont-de-Montvert on 12 August 1702, but the revolt spread. Its fighters, called Camisards, perhaps from the white shirts (camisa in Occitan) worn on night raids, formed several bands under Rolland, Jean Cavalier, Abraham Mazel, Nicolas Jouany and others. At its height the movement may have had 2,000–3,000 fighters, supported by much of the Protestant population.

The Camisards fought a guerrilla war in the mountains and the plains around Alès, Anduze and Nîmes. They ambushed troops, burned churches and presbyteries, and killed priests and Catholic villagers, as in the attack on Fraissinet-de-Fourques in February 1703, which left around forty dead. Royal forces under Marshal Montrevel and the intendant Basville answered with summary executions, the breaking of rebels on the wheel and burnings. On 1 April 1703, Palm Sunday, Montrevel's troops surrounded a mill at the Agau gate of Nîmes where Protestants had gathered for worship, set it on fire and killed those who tried to escape. Catholic irregulars, known as the 'cadets of the Cross' or 'white Camisards', raided and massacred in Protestant villages.

From September to December 1703 the crown carried out the 'grand brûlement des Cévennes': the inhabitants of some 466 villages and hamlets in the upper Cévennes were ordered to leave, and their homes, crops and livestock were destroyed to deprive the rebels of support. In March 1704 Cavalier defeated royal troops at Martignargues, but his band was routed at Nages in April. The new commander, Marshal Villars, combined military pressure with offers of amnesty. In May 1704 Cavalier negotiated with Villars at Nîmes and agreed to surrender in return for a commission and permission for his men to leave France; his followers, who had fought for the restoration of their worship, regarded this as betrayal. Rolland was killed in August 1704 near the château of Castelnau, and his body was dragged through Nîmes and burned.

Most remaining leaders surrendered or were captured in 1704–05; a plot to renew the rising in 1705 ended with the execution of Ravanel and Catinat at Nîmes. Abraham Mazel, who escaped and returned, led a last attempt in the Vivarais in 1709 and was killed in 1710. In 1715 the young preacher Antoine Court held the first synod of the 'Church of the Desert', rejecting prophetic inspiration and armed resistance in favour of rebuilding a disciplined Reformed church under persecution. French Protestants gained civil status only with the Edict of Versailles in 1787 and full freedom of worship during the Revolution.

Several Camisard prophets, including Élie Marion, reached London in 1706, where the 'French Prophets' caused a sensation and won English followers; their ecstatic practice has been linked to later movements, including the Shakers. In France the Camisards became a symbol of Protestant memory and of resistance to tyranny. Since 1911 an annual assembly has gathered at the Mas Soubeyran in Mialet, Rolland's birthplace and now the Musée du Désert.
conflicts/camisard-war/nameOfGod: The Camisards called themselves the 'Children of God' and the 'troops of the Lord'. Their prophets, believed to be moved by the Holy Spirit, chose targets, judged traitors and ordered attacks, and the fighters went into battle singing Psalm 68 in Clément Marot's version, 'Que Dieu se montre seulement', known as the 'Psalm of battles'. They saw themselves as Israel fighting the idolaters and burned churches as houses of idolatry. Bishop Esprit Fléchier of Nîmes and royal officials condemned them as 'fanatics' and treated their inspiration as madness or imposture. Catholic militias wore crosses and called themselves the 'cadets of the Cross'; rumours that they acted under a papal bull of Clement XI granting indulgences circulated at the time, but no such bull has been found and the claim is generally doubted.
conflicts/camisard-war/religiousCauses/0: The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 outlawed Protestant worship and forced Huguenots to conform outwardly to Catholicism.
conflicts/camisard-war/religiousCauses/1: Forced attendance at Mass, the seizure of children for Catholic education and the punishment of secret assemblies created intense resentment.
conflicts/camisard-war/religiousCauses/2: A prophetic and apocalyptic movement convinced many that God was calling them to overthrow 'Babylon' and restore true worship.
conflicts/camisard-war/religiousCauses/3: The abbé du Chaila's mission work and imprisonment of would-be emigrants made him a symbol of religious coercion.
conflicts/camisard-war/religiousCauses/4: Executions of preachers such as Claude Brousson and of prophets fed a culture of martyrdom and resistance.
conflicts/camisard-war/otherCauses/0: Heavy war taxation, including the capitation introduced in 1695 during Louis XIV's wars, burdened a poor mountain population.
conflicts/camisard-war/otherCauses/1: The rugged terrain of the Cévennes favoured guerrilla warfare and made royal control difficult.
conflicts/camisard-war/otherCauses/2: Regional resentment of the intendant Basville's authoritarian administration of Languedoc.
conflicts/camisard-war/otherCauses/3: France's involvement in the War of the Spanish Succession tied down royal troops and encouraged hopes of help from Protestant England and the Dutch Republic.
conflicts/camisard-war/triggers/0: The killing of the abbé du Chaila at Le Pont-de-Montvert on the night of 24 July 1702.
conflicts/camisard-war/triggers/1: The execution of Esprit Séguier on 12 August 1702, which spread the revolt.
conflicts/camisard-war/triggers/2: The intensification of military repression of secret assemblies and prophets in the Cévennes in the spring and summer of 1702.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/0/text: Edict of Fontainebleau revokes the Edict of Nantes.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/1/text: Prophetic movement spreads from the Dauphiné into the Vivarais and Cévennes.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/2/text: The lay preacher Claude Brousson is executed at Montpellier.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/3/text: Abbé du Chaila killed at Le Pont-de-Montvert (July); Esprit Séguier burned (August).
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/4/text: Massacre at the mill of the Agau, Nîmes (April); 'grand brûlement' of the upper Cévennes (September–December).
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/5/text: Cavalier victorious at Martignargues and defeated at Nages; he submits to Villars in May; Rolland killed in August.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/6/text: Failed plot to renew the rising; Ravanel and Catinat executed at Nîmes.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/7/text: Camisard prophets arrive in London as the 'French Prophets'.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/8/text: Abraham Mazel is killed after a last attempt at revolt.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/9/text: Antoine Court holds the first synod of the Church of the Desert.
conflicts/camisard-war/timeline/10/text: Edict of Versailles grants Protestants civil status.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/0/role: Camisard commander in the plain of Languedoc
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/0/focus: A baker's apprentice who became the most gifted Camisard general, he won several engagements and then negotiated his surrender with Villars in 1704.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/0/outco: Left France, served in the British army at Almansa (1707) and died as lieutenant-governor of Jersey; many former comrades regarded his surrender as betrayal.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/1/focus: Led the Camisards of the upper Cévennes and refused all compromise without restoration of Protestant worship.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/1/outco: Betrayed and killed near Castelnau in August 1704; his house at the Mas Soubeyran is now the Musée du Désert.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/2/role: Prophet and leader of the first rising
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/2/focus: Led the attack on the abbé du Chaila at Le Pont-de-Montvert, declaring that the Spirit had commanded it.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/2/outco: Captured and burned alive on 12 August 1702.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/3/focus: Took part in the attack on du Chaila and continued resistance after others had submitted, escaping from prison in 1705.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/3/outco: Killed in 1710 after a final attempt at revolt in the Vivarais.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/4/name: Abbé François de Langlade du Chaila
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/4/role: Archpriest of the Cévennes and inspector of missions
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/4/focus: Directed the forcible conversion of Protestants and imprisoned those who tried to flee or worship.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/4/outco: Killed at Le Pont-de-Montvert on 24 July 1702, the act that began the war.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/5/focus: Organised the repression of Protestant worship, the punishment of rebels and the road network built to control the Cévennes.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/5/outco: Remained in office until 1718; remembered by Protestants as the 'tyrant of Languedoc'.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/6/focus: Combined force with amnesty and negotiation, securing Cavalier's surrender.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/6/outco: Went on to command in the War of the Spanish Succession, winning at Denain in 1712.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/7/focus: Fought in the Cévennes and, after surrendering in 1704, went into exile.
conflicts/camisard-war/keyPeople/7/outco: Became one of the 'French Prophets' in London and travelled on prophetic missions across Europe; died at Livorno.
conflicts/camisard-war/casualties/note: No reliable overall estimate exists. Contemporary and later accounts suggest that several thousand people died on each side, including Catholic priests and villagers killed by the Camisards and Protestant civilians killed by troops and Catholic militias; hundreds more were executed and thousands imprisoned, sent to the galleys or deported. The destruction of some 466 villages and hamlets in 1703 displaced a large part of the upland population. Figures in older literature vary widely and are largely impressionistic.
conflicts/camisard-war/effects/0: Louis XIV had to divert thousands of troops, including a marshal of France, from the War of the Spanish Succession to suppress the revolt.
conflicts/camisard-war/effects/1: The upper Cévennes was devastated by the 'grand brûlement', and the crown built military roads and forts to control the region.
conflicts/camisard-war/effects/2: The failure of armed resistance led French Protestants to adopt a strategy of patient, disciplined survival under the Church of the Desert.
conflicts/camisard-war/effects/3: The revolt drew European attention to the persecution of French Protestants and became part of the case for toleration made by later writers.
conflicts/camisard-war/effectsOnChurch/0: Antoine Court and his successors rebuilt French Reformed churches through clandestine synods and pastors trained at the seminary in Lausanne, rejecting prophetic ecstasy.
conflicts/camisard-war/effectsOnChurch/1: The Camisard prophets carried an ecstatic, charismatic piety to England and elsewhere, influencing radical and revivalist groups.
conflicts/camisard-war/effectsOnChurch/2: Catholic coercion in the Cévennes failed to produce genuine conversions, and the region has remained a Protestant heartland.
conflicts/camisard-war/effectsOnChurch/3: The memory of the Desert and the Camisards became central to French Protestant identity, celebrated annually at the Mas Soubeyran.
conflicts/camisard-war/legacy: The Camisard War was the last major war of religion in France. It showed both the limits of royal power to compel belief and the dangers of a resistance driven by prophecy. French Protestants long held an ambivalent memory of it, honouring the Camisards' courage while choosing Antoine Court's non-violent path; historians debate how far it was a religious war, a peasant revolt or an early struggle for freedom of conscience.
conflicts/camisard-war/dissenters/0/text: Born in the Vivarais in 1695 and shaped by the aftermath of the war, Court rejected both the prophets' claims to inspiration and the use of arms, holding the first synod of the Desert in 1715 and rebuilding the church through preaching, discipline and patience under persecution.
conflicts/camisard-war/dissenters/1/text: The lawyer turned preacher urged Protestants to keep worshipping despite the law, but insisted on spiritual rather than armed resistance; he was executed at Montpellier in 1698, before the revolt, and became a model of non-violent martyrdom.
conflicts/camisard-war/dissenters/2/text: The exiled Reformed pastor in the Dutch Republic urged French Protestants to remain faithful to their religion while obeying their sovereign, and later published a pastoral instruction (around 1719) on obedience to the sovereign, reflecting the unease of many Refuge pastors about the Camisards' violence.
conflicts/camisard-war/theatres/0/name: Le Pont-de-Montvert, killing of du Chaila
conflicts/camisard-war/campaigns/0/title: Jean Cavalier's path from rebellion to exile
conflicts/camisard-war/campaigns/0/text: After negotiating with Villars at Nîmes, Cavalier left France, deserted to Switzerland, raised a regiment of Huguenot refugees for the allies, fought at Almansa in Spain in 1707 and ended his career in British service as lieutenant-governor of Jersey.
conflicts/camisard-war/campaigns/1/text: Marion surrendered in 1704 and went into exile in Switzerland; in London from 1706 he and other Camisard prophets prophesied publicly, before setting out on missionary journeys across Europe that ended with his death in Italy.
